slides.title: Why frontend security is different
slides.summary: Your code runs on a machine you don't control, next to code you didn't write. The browser is the security boundary.
body: On the server, you control the machine. In the browser, you ship your code to the user and it runs alongside extensions, other tabs, third-party scripts and whatever an attacker can get onto the page.

ul: Nothing in the bundle is secret. Anyone can read your JavaScript, API keys and feature flags in DevTools.
Every check can be skipped. A user can edit requests, call your API directly or change any value in memory.
The page mixes trust levels. Your code, user content, ads, analytics and npm packages all share one origin.

body: <mark>Client-side checks are for user experience. Every security decision must be enforced again on the server.</mark>

body.note: A shop window: you decide what's on display, but anyone walking past can look at it, and the till must still be behind the counter.

items.label: Confidentiality
items.sub: Keep data away from people who shouldn't see it: tokens, PII, other users' data.

items.label: Integrity
items.sub: Make sure only the user and your code can change things: no injected scripts, no forged requests.

items.label: Availability
items.sub: Keep the app usable: no malicious script that freezes the page or locks users out.

viz.html: The classic CIA triad applies in the browser too.

slides.title: Origins: the browser's unit of trust
slides.summary: An origin is scheme + host + port. The same-origin policy stops one origin reading another's data.
body: Browsers isolate sites by origin: the scheme, host and port of a URL. Two URLs share an origin only if all three match.
The same-origin policy (SOP) lets a page freely read data from its own origin, but blocks it from reading responses, storage and DOM that belong to another origin.

ul: Blocked: reading a cross-origin fetch response, another origin's localStorage, or the DOM of a cross-origin iframe.
Allowed: sending requests, form posts, and embedding images, scripts, styles and iframes from other origins.

body: <mark>The SOP stops reads, not writes. That gap is why CSRF exists, and why CORS is needed to relax reads safely.</mark>

body.text: A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (eTLD+1), so app.example.com and api.example.com are the same site but different origins. Cookies' SameSite attribute works on sites; the SOP works on origins.

slides.title: The map of this section
slides.summary: Frontend security is defence in depth: several independent layers, so one mistake isn't fatal.
body: No single control stops every attack. Good frontends stack layers, so an attacker has to beat several of them at once.

ul: Keep attackers' code out: encode output, sanitize HTML, validate input.
Limit what injected code can do: CSP, Trusted Types, Permissions-Policy, HttpOnly cookies.
Control who can embed or call you: frame-ancestors, CORS, SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens.
Trust your supply chain: lockfiles, audits, SRI.
Protect data in transit and at rest: HTTPS, HSTS, careful client storage, and the law around personal data.
